props.title: The Invisible Woman

sections.content: The screwball comedy meets science fiction in The Invisible Woman, a lighthearted spin on H.G. Wells' invisible person concept that followed Universal's darker treatments The Invisible Man (1933) and The Invisible Man Returns (1940). Director A. Edward Sutherland transforms the typically horror-focused invisibility premise into a romantic comedy, with Virginia Bruce starring as fashion model Kitty Carroll who volunteers for an eccentric scientist's invisibility experiment. The film marked a significant departure from Universal's monster movie formula, instead embracing the screwball elements popular in late 1930s cinema like Bringing Up Baby (1938) and The Awful Truth (1937).

sections.content: The film's special effects by John P. Fulton, who also worked on The Invisible Man (1933), were groundbreaking for their time. While modern viewers might find the techniques dated, the combination of practical effects, wire work, and optical printing created convincing invisibility sequences that influenced later films like Abbott and Costello Meet the Invisible Man (1951) and even modern interpretations like Hollow Man (2000). The comedy-focused approach to invisibility would later be echoed in films like Now You See Him, Now You Don't (1972) and Memoirs of an Invisible Man (1992).

What makes The Invisible Woman particularly noteworthy is its feminist undertones, unusual for its era. Kitty uses her invisibility not for revenge or violence like her male counterparts, but to stand up to her abusive boss and help others. This theme of women using extraordinary abilities to overcome societal constraints would later emerge in films like Miss Congeniality (2000) and Wonder Woman (2017), though with less subtle messaging. sections.content: The film's blend of science fiction elements with romantic comedy created a template that later films would follow, including The Incredible Shrinking Woman (1981) and Date with an Angel (1987). Its lighter approach to fantastic elements influenced how Hollywood would handle sci-fi concepts in family-friendly films throughout the 1940s and beyond, seen in movies like The Ghost and Mrs. Muir (1947) and Bell Book and Candle (1958).
